title: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules — 2024
subject: chemistry
topicTitle: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules — 2024
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: State the main postulates of VSEPR theory. Use it to predict the shape of CH₄.
questions.solution:
**VSEPR:** electron pairs (bond + lone) repel and arrange to maximise separation; repulsion order lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp.

CH₄ has 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → pairs point to tetrahedron corners → **tetrahedral**, 109.5°.
questions.knowledgeNote: Count steric number (pairs) first, then hide lone pairs to read the molecular shape.

questions.question: Predict the shapes of BF₃ and PCl₅ using VSEPR theory. Give their hybridisation.
questions.solution:
**BF₃:** 3 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → **trigonal planar**, 120°, sp² hybridised B.

**PCl₅:** 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → **trigonal bipyramidal** (3 equatorial at 120°, 2 axial at 90°), sp³d hybridised P.
questions.knowledgeNote: Axial bonds (90° repulsions) are longer and weaker than equatorial — PCl₅'s axial Cl leaves first.

questions.question: Explain why H₂O is bent while CO₂ is linear, though oxygen is the central atom in neither case the same way.
questions.solution:
**H₂O:** O carries 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs — lone pairs compress the angle to **104.5° (bent)**.

**CO₂:** C carries 2 bond pairs + 0 lone pairs — pairs oppose diametrically → **180° (linear)**.

Shape follows the lone-pair count, not the atoms present.
questions.knowledgeNote: 2 pairs → linear; 3 → trigonal planar; 4 → tetrahedral electron geometry — then subtract lone pairs for shape.

questions.question: What is hybridisation? Show how sp³ hybridisation explains the shape of methane.
questions.solution:
**Hybridisation** mixes atomic orbitals into equal-energy hybrids aimed at bonding directions.

Carbon's 2s + three 2p blend into **four sp³ hybrids** pointing to tetrahedron corners (109.5°). Each overlaps a H 1s orbital → four equal C–H bonds, tetrahedral CH₄.
questions.knowledgeNote: Hybridisation follows observed shape (it rationalises, never predicts alone) — VSEPR first, hybrids second.

questions.question: Predict the shape and hybridisation of SF₆ and IF₇.
questions.solution:
**SF₆:** 6 bond pairs → **octahedral**, 90°, sp³d² hybridised S.

**IF₇:** 7 bond pairs → **pentagonal bipyramidal**, sp³d³ hybridised I.
questions.knowledgeNote: Expanded octets need d-orbitals (period 3+) — period-2 elements stop at four pairs.

questions.question: Ammonia has a higher boiling point than phosphine (PH₃). Explain on the basis of molecular shape and bonding.
questions.solution:
NH₃ is pyramidal with a strongly polar N–H bond and a lone pair — molecules link by **hydrogen bonding**, needing much heat to separate (bp −33°C).

PH₃ is larger, less electronegative, barely H-bonded — weak van der Waals forces only (bp −88°C). Shape concentrates the dipole that H-bonding requires.
questions.knowledgeNote: Same-group hydride anomalies (H₂O, HF, NH₃ high boilers) are all hydrogen-bonding verdicts.
